title: Why Foam Does Not Always Equal Cleaning Power
excerpt: Foam is a visible property of a cleaning solution, but the amount of foam does not directly measure how well the product removes soil.
content_html:
Foam is easy to see, so it is often mistaken for evidence that a cleaner is working harder. In reality, foam is mainly a physical behaviour of the formulation. Cleaning performance depends on soil removal, wetting, chemistry, mechanical action and recovery—not on the height of the bubbles.

Why cleaners foam

Some surfactants stabilise air bubbles in water more readily than others. Agitation, water conditions, concentration and the presence of soil can also change how much foam appears.

High foam can clean well—or poorly

A high-foaming product may perform well for one task, while a low-foaming product may be better for another. Many machine-cleaning systems are designed around controlled or low foam because excessive foam can interfere with recovery or equipment operation.

Appearance is not a measurement

Foam level does not directly measure concentration, surfactant activity or soil removal. Judging a product by bubbles can therefore lead to incorrect conclusions about whether the solution is too weak or too strong.

Formulators choose foam deliberately

EPA recognises defoamers and surfactants as different functional ingredient classes. This reflects an important formulation principle: foam level can be adjusted independently from other cleaning functions.

Follow the product design

Use a product according to its label and equipment compatibility requirements. Do not add extra concentrate simply to produce more visible foam.

Practical takeaway

Foam is a formulation characteristic, not a cleaning-power gauge. The meaningful result is whether the approved process removes the target soil without damaging the surface or interfering with the equipment.

References

  1. US EPA — Safer Choice Standard and Criteria.
  2. CDC — Cleaning Supplies and Equipment.
